html:
The encomienda was the Spanish system that gave conquerors and settlers in the Americas the labour and tribute of a group of Indigenous people. The holder was supposed to protect them and teach them Christianity; in practice it was often close to slavery.

It began on Hispaniola, where the Taíno were handed out to work mines and fields and died in huge numbers. Friars protested, and the Laws of Burgos of 1512 tried to soften the system. It spread with the conquest to Mexico, Peru and Central America, to peoples such as the Huetar of Costa Rica and the Huarpe, many marched over the Andes to Chile.

Bartolomé de las Casas, once an encomendero himself, became its fiercest critic. The New Laws of 1542 banned new grants. Settlers resisted, but the system slowly gave way to royal labour drafts and debt labour on estates.
